actions.justification: First priority in any behavioral emergency is ensuring the safety of the environment for staff and patient before approaching.
Mandatory baseline vital signs assessment to identify any physiological instability contributing to the presentation.
Mandatory assessment to rule out organic/medical causes of behavioral disturbance (e.g., hypoxia, infection, metabolic derangement, intoxication).
Mandatory action - verbal de-escalation is the first-line approach for agitated/behavioral patients, prioritizing least restrictive intervention before considering medications or restraints.
Mandatory action - hypoglycemia is a reversible medical cause of altered behavior/agitation that must be ruled out immediately as it is easily treatable.
Formal assessment of aggression level guides the appropriate level of intervention needed (verbal, pharmacological, or physical restraint) and helps tailor the management plan.
Substance intoxication or withdrawal is a common reversible cause of agitation/behavioral disturbance; assessment guides appropriate medication choice and management.
After initial assessment and de-escalation attempts, selecting an appropriate sedating/antipsychotic medication is the next step if agitation persists and medical causes have been assessed.
Verbal de-escalation should continue as the least restrictive intervention while further workup and medication selection are underway.

Patient has been assessed for aggression level and verbal de-escalation has been attempted/continued. If the patient remains agitated or poses a safety risk, applying the least restrictive restraint is the next appropriate step per psychiatric emergency guidelines, prioritizing patient and staff safety.
Documentation of clinical indication for any restraint is mandatory for legal, ethical, and regulatory compliance when restraint is applied or considered.

If serotonin syndrome is suspected (based on medication history, substance use assessment, and clinical presentation), cyproheptadine is the first-line pharmacologic treatment as a serotonin antagonist.

Lorazepam is a first-line benzodiazepine for agitation management and can help with sedation while remaining safer than antipsychotics if serotonin syndrome is a concern (cyproheptadine already given). Helps reduce agitation and muscle activity.
IV fluid resuscitation supports hemodynamic stability, aids in preventing rhabdomyolysis if neuromuscular hyperactivity is present, and maintains renal perfusion.

Given the clinical complexity (cyproheptadine already given suggesting serotonin syndrome concern, restraints applied, ongoing agitation management), ICU admission is warranted for close monitoring of vital signs, neurological status, and potential deterioration.
